steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the "Goals" section of a Wikipedia article on anytime algorithms: what they are meant to achieve, why they matter for AI, a couple of examples, and what sets them apart (being interruptible and improving with more time).

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Goal: better quality results in return for turn-around time
- Examples
- What makes them unique: many possible outcomes, quality measures
- Use for large decision set problems; comparison with dynamic programming
- Interruptible: stop at any time, return best result so far

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Goal
  - give intelligent systems ability to make results of better quality in return for turn-around time
  - flexible in time and resources
  - important: AI algorithms can take a long time to complete results; this is designed to complete in shorter time
  - better understanding that system is dependent and restricted to its agents, how they work cooperatively
- Examples
  - Newton–Raphson iteration for square root of a number
  - trajectory problems, aiming for a target: object moving through space while algorithm runs; approximate answer given early can significantly improve accuracy
- What makes them unique
  - can return many possible outcomes for any given input
  - many well defined quality measures to monitor progress in problem solving and distributed computing resources
  - keeps searching for best possible answer with the time it is given
  - may not run until completion; may improve the answer if allowed to run longer
- Large decision set problems
  - often used for these; otherwise generally no useful info unless allowed to finish
  - sounds similar to dynamic programming, but fine-tuned through random adjustments, not sequential
- Interruptible
  - can be told to stop at any time, returns best result found so far
  - hence "interruptible algorithm"
  - some maintain the last result, so with more time they continue from where they left off for an even better result

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
The goal of anytime algorithms is to let intelligent systems make results of better quality in return for turn-around time. They should also be flexible in time and resources. They matter because AI algorithms (artificial intelligence algorithms) can take a long time to complete results, and this kind of algorithm is designed to complete in a shorter time. They are also meant to give a better understanding that the system is dependent and restricted to its agents and how the agents work cooperatively. One example is the Newton–Raphson iteration used for finding the square root of a number. Another example is trajectory problems when you are aiming for a target, where the object is moving through space while it waits for the algorithm to finish, and even an approximate answer can improve its accuracy a lot if it is given early.

What is unique about anytime algorithms is that they can return many possible outcomes for any given input. An anytime algorithm uses many well defined quality measures to monitor the progress in problem solving and distributed computing resources. It keeps on searching for the best possible answer with the amount of time it is given. It may not run until completion, and it may improve the answer if it is allowed to run longer.

- often used for large decision set problems; these generally give no useful info unless allowed to finish
- similar to dynamic programming? difference: fine-tuned through random adjustments, not sequential
- can be told to stop at any time -> best result found so far; so called interruptible algorithm
- some keep the last result so with more time they continue where they left off -> even better result

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
The goal of anytime algorithms is to let intelligent systems make results of better quality in return for turn-around time. They should also be flexible in time and resources. They matter because AI algorithms (artificial intelligence algorithms) can take a long time to complete results, and this kind of algorithm is designed to complete in a shorter time. They are also meant to give a better understanding that the system is dependent and restricted to its agents and how the agents work cooperatively. One example is the Newton–Raphson iteration used for finding the square root of a number. Another example is trajectory problems when you are aiming for a target, where the object is moving through space while it waits for the algorithm to finish, and even an approximate answer can improve its accuracy a lot if it is given early.

What is unique about anytime algorithms is that they can return many possible outcomes for any given input. An anytime algorithm uses many well defined quality measures to monitor the progress in problem solving and distributed computing resources. It keeps on searching for the best possible answer with the amount of time it is given. It may not run until completion, and it may improve the answer if it is allowed to run longer.

This is often used for problems with large decision sets. Such problems would generally not give useful information unless the algorithm is allowed to finish. This may sound similar to dynamic programming, but the difference is that it is fine-tuned through random adjustments and not sequentially.

Anytime algorithms are designed so that they can be told to stop at any time and then they return the best result they found so far. That is why it is called an interruptible algorithm. Some anytime algorithms also keep the last result, so if they are given more time they can continue from where they left off and get an even better result.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The goal of anytime algorithms is to give intelligent systems the ability to make results of better quality in return for turn-around time. They are also meant to be flexible in time and resources.[1] They are important because artificial intelligence or AI algorithms can take a long time to complete results, and this algorithm is designed to complete in a shorter amount of time.[1] They are also intended to give a better understanding that the system is dependent and restricted to its agents and how they work cooperatively.[1] An example is the Newton–Raphson iteration applied to finding the square root of a number.[2] Another example that uses anytime algorithms is trajectory problems when you are aiming for a target; the object is moving through space while waiting for the algorithm to finish, and even an approximate answer can significantly improve its accuracy if it is given early.[1]

What makes anytime algorithms unique is their ability to return many possible outcomes for any given input. An anytime algorithm uses many well defined quality measures to monitor progress in problem solving and distributed computing resources. It keeps searching for the best possible answer with the amount of time it is given.[3] It may not run until completion, and may improve the answer if it is allowed to run longer.[4]

This is often used for large decision set problems, which would generally not provide useful information unless allowed to finish.[5] While this may sound similar to dynamic programming, the difference is that it is fine-tuned through random adjustments rather than sequentially.

Anytime algorithms are designed so that they can be told to stop at any time and return the best result found so far.[1] This is why it is called an interruptible algorithm. Certain anytime algorithms also maintain the last result, so that if given more time they can continue from where they left off to obtain an even better result.[1]
